debug.title: A comment swallows the page

interview.q: Walk me through what happens between typing a URL and seeing the page.
interview.answer: The browser resolves the host with DNS, opens a connection and negotiates TLS, sends an HTTP request, receives the response, parses HTML into the DOM, fetches CSS and scripts, builds the render tree, lays out boxes and paints, then runs scripts that may change the DOM.

interview.q: Is HTML a programming language? How do you answer that in an interview?
interview.answer: HTML is a markup language: it describes structure and meaning, with no variables, control flow or computation. The honest answer names what it is, then points out that the platform as a whole — HTML, CSS and JavaScript — is programmable.

interview.q: When would you choose a static page over a dynamic one?
interview.answer: When the content changes rarely and is the same for every visitor: static files cache well, cost less to serve and are easy to audit. A dynamic page is worth it when the response depends on the user, the data or the request.

debug.title: The script runs before the button exists

interview.q: Why is index.html the entry point?
interview.answer: It is the conventional directory index: a server maps a request for a folder to index.html, and every hosting platform supports it without configuration.

interview.q: What is the difference between opening a file with file:// and serving it over HTTP?
interview.answer: A file URL has no origin, so modules, fetch and some storage APIs are restricted. Over HTTP the page has an origin, relative requests work the way they will in production, and cookies and service workers are available.

interview.q: Which files belong in a project root?
interview.answer: The entry document, the project configuration and top-level folders such as css, js, images and assets. Build output and dependencies stay out of version control.

debug.title: Charset declared too late
debug.error: Late charset: the browser has already decoded text before reading the declaration, so non-ASCII characters can arrive corrupted.

debug.title: Head is never closed
debug.error: Missing closing head tag: the parser closes it implicitly at body, which hides a structural mistake that a validator would report.

interview.q: What does the browser do before it renders anything?
interview.answer: It decodes the bytes, tokenises the markup, builds the DOM, discovers stylesheets and scripts, and only then computes styles and layout. Rendering waits on blocking resources it finds in the head.

interview.q: Why is the doctype not an element?
interview.answer: It is a document type declaration that selects standards mode. It has no content, no closing tag and no node in the DOM tree.

interview.q: What belongs in head versus body?
interview.answer: Head holds metadata and resource declarations: charset, title, description, stylesheets, scripts. Body holds the content the visitor sees and interacts with.

debug.title: An unquoted value with a space
debug.error: Unquoted attribute value: the parser stops the value at the space, so the element gets an incomplete class list.

debug.title: A data attribute written in camelCase
debug.error: Attribute names are lowercased by the parser, so a script reading dataset.userId never matches data-userId in the source.

interview.q: What is the difference between an attribute and a property?
interview.answer: The attribute is what the markup declares; the property is the live value on the DOM object. They start equal but diverge: typing in an input changes the property, not the attribute.

interview.q: When should you use a data-* attribute instead of a class?
interview.answer: When the value is data for behaviour or configuration rather than a styling hook. Classes describe presentation patterns; data attributes carry values that scripts read.

interview.q: Name three global attributes you actually use and say why.
interview.answer: id for unique targets and labels, class for reusable styling hooks, and lang for language changes inside a document. Others worth naming are hidden, title, tabindex and data-*.

debug.title: Bold used where importance is meant
debug.error: b is a visual offset with no importance; strong carries the meaning that assistive technology and search tools can read.

debug.title: An unescaped angle bracket in code
debug.error: A raw less-than sign inside code starts a tag, so the parser drops or rearranges the rest of the snippet.

interview.q: When is the br element the right choice?
interview.answer: When the line break is part of the content: an address, a poem, a short piece of dialogue. It is not a spacing tool; margins belong to CSS.

interview.q: strong versus b, em versus i — what is the difference?
interview.answer: strong and em carry semantic stress or importance; b and i are presentational offsets. They can look identical, but only the semantic pair is announced and interpreted.

interview.q: How do you mark up a code snippet that contains angle brackets?
interview.answer: Use pre and code and escape the less-than sign as an entity and the ampersand as its entity. Otherwise the parser treats the snippet as markup.

interview.q: How does the browser resolve a relative URL?
interview.answer: Against the document’s base URL: the directory of the current page unless a base element says otherwise. That is why the same href resolves differently on pages in different folders.

interview.q: What is reverse tabnabbing and how do you prevent it?
interview.answer: A page opened with target blank can reach window.opener and navigate the original tab. The noopener relationship removes that reference; noreferrer also hides the referrer.

interview.q: How would you structure navigation for a ten-page site?
interview.answer: One shared nav with a short, stable set of top-level links, current-page indication, a skip link before it, and consistent order on every page. Deeper pages get breadcrumbs rather than more top-level items.

debug.title: Description list built from list items
debug.error: Wrong children: dl pairs dt with dd; li is not allowed, so the term and description relation is lost.

interview.q: Why should a navigation menu be a list of links?
interview.answer: A list groups the items so assistive technology announces the count and the boundaries, and each link keeps its own destination. Styling with CSS does not require giving up the structure.

interview.q: ol, ul or dl — how do you choose?
interview.answer: ol when order changes the meaning, ul when it does not, dl when you are pairing terms with descriptions.

interview.q: How does a screen reader announce a list?
interview.answer: It announces the list and its item count, then each item. That context disappears when a list is replaced with plain links or divs.

interview.q: How do you write alt text for a chart?
interview.answer: State the message the chart carries, not its shape: what is compared, the direction of the change and the range. If the exact numbers matter, provide them in a table next to it.

interview.q: What does srcset actually let the browser decide?
interview.answer: Which candidate resource to download, based on viewport width, pixel density and the sizes declaration. The author supplies candidates; the browser picks, and it may pick differently after a resize.

interview.q: Why can lazy loading hurt the largest contentful paint?
interview.answer: A lazy image in the initial viewport is not fetched until layout discovers it, which delays the largest paint. Hero images should load eagerly; below-the-fold images are the lazy ones.

debug.title: A merged cell with an extra neighbour
debug.error: Column overflow: the row declares three columns while the header has two, so the table grid no longer lines up.

debug.title: A layout built from a table
debug.error: No data relationship: a layout table creates meaningless row and column context for assistive technology and cannot reflow like block content.

interview.q: How do you make a table accessible?
interview.answer: Add a caption, use header cells with scope col or row, keep one header per column or row, avoid layout tables, and make sure merged cells still leave every row with the right number of columns.

interview.q: When is a table the wrong element?
interview.answer: For page layout, for lists of unrelated items, and for anything that needs to reflow as a single column on a phone. If there is no row-and-column relationship, it is not tabular data.

interview.q: What pitfalls come with rowspan and colspan?
interview.answer: They change the grid, so later rows must supply the remaining cells; screen readers rely on the resulting header relationships, and responsive CSS cannot simply stack cells without breaking the pairing.

debug.title: A section used only for spacing
debug.error: Section without a heading and without a theme is just a container: it adds a region with no accessible name.

debug.title: The page footer nested inside main
debug.error: Footer inside main describes the main content, not the page, so the site-wide footer landmark disappears.

interview.q: How do landmarks help keyboard and screen-reader users?
interview.answer: They expose the page’s regions to a landmark list, so a user can jump straight to main, navigation, search or the footer instead of tabbing through everything.

interview.q: section, article or div — how do you decide?
interview.answer: Article if the content stands alone and could be syndicated; section if it is a themed part of the page that has a heading; div if it is only a styling or scripting container.

interview.q: Does semantic HTML improve SEO? What actually matters?
interview.answer: Semantics make the structure unambiguous for crawlers, but ranking is driven by content quality, links, performance and intent matching. Semantic markup helps interpretation and accessibility more than it moves rankings by itself.
